guide/flexboard-storyboard-guide.title: FLEXBOARD Storyboards in 7 Steps - AI Video Production Workflow
guide/flexboard-storyboard-guide.summary: How to make a cut-by-cut storyboard from one scenario, fix only the cuts that have problems, and hand it to Seedance 2.5 - the FLEXBOARD workflow in seven steps.

blocks.text: **What this article covers**: how to make a cut-by-cut storyboard from one scenario, fix only the cuts that have problems, and hand it over to Seedance 2.5
**Who it is for**: people making AI video for the first time, and anyone who has burned credits re-rolling video

**What you need**: an XCONDA account with credits, one scene of your scenario and, if you have one, a background image made in Turn. The credit cost is shown on the image generation and regenerate buttons.
This is the storyboard episode of the AI video production workflow series. It uses the backgrounds and key images made in the previous post, "Building a 360-degree set with XCONDA Turn".

**Where is FLEXBOARD**

In XCONDA, open Studio then Storyboard from the left menu and the FLEXBOARD card appears — the one labelled "a storyboard tool tuned for Seedance 2.5". Click the card and choose New Project.
**Step 1: Project settings**
The top of the screen shows the three working stages as buttons.

items: **Project settings**: the basic setup of the project
**Scene Settings**: scenario, cast and backgrounds, number of cuts
**Edit Panel**: review and fix the cuts you generated

blocks.text: Steps 1-5 of this article live in the first two buttons; steps 6-7 live in Edit Panel. Start with three choices.

items: **Working method**
**Image model**: pick the model that draws the cut images from the dropdown at the top left. Four models are available today.
**Project name**: something you can find in the list later. Example: "webdrama_ep1_daecheongmaru_scene"

blocks.text: **Step 2: Write the scenario, genre and mood**
Write the scene in the **Scenario** field. If it answers who, where, what and with what feeling, the cuts are easier to review. When several things happen, write them in order.
For example:

A rainy night on a hanok's wooden veranda. Suyeon stands holding a shard of broken pottery. Footsteps approach from the gate and she hides the shard behind her back. The door opens and her mother walks in. The two look at each other without a word.
Then choose **Genre** (for example, Suspense) and **Tone / Mood** (for example, Tense), and save with **Save project**.
**Step 3: Register the cast and backgrounds (Reference Assets)**
This is the step that keeps the same person and the same place across cuts. In the **Reference Assets** area you register **Cast** cards and **Background** cards.

items: Click **Add Cast** to create a cast card. Each card automatically gets a label (a token) such as **@image1** or **@image2**.
Add a face image and an easy-to-recognise name to the card. Example: Suyeon, Mother
Props that come back can be registered as cards too. Example: broken pottery
Add a Background card. This is a good place for the space image you made in Turn in the previous post.

blocks.text: **What the tokens do**: a cut description shows "@image1", so you can see at a glance who appears in that cut. Video prompts point at characters the same way.
**Caution**: register one card per person. After you replace or delete a card, check again that the token numbers still match the cut descriptions.
**Step 4: Set the number of cuts and the shot length**

items: **Number of Panels**: how many cuts you want. The example screen uses 9.
**Shot Length**: the length of one cut, adjustable between 4 and 30 seconds.

blocks.text: For example, 9 cuts x 15 seconds adds up to about 2 minutes 15 seconds. The finished length depends on what you do in the video stage.

Choose cut counts at the points where the scene changes. With the example above you could split it as "Suyeon holding the pottery / footsteps / the hand hiding it / the door opens / the mother enters / the two facing each other".
**Step 5: Check the text before you spend on images (Text Preview)**
Press the yellow **Text Preview Generate** button at the bottom of the screen and you get a written storyboard for each cut before any image is made. On each CUT card, check three things.

items: Do the scene descriptions come in the order you intended?
Do the @image tokens point at the right people?
Does the SFX note underneath match the mood of the scene?

blocks.text: If the cut order, the cast or the transitions feel wrong, go back to the scenario or the cut count and fix it **before you generate images**. Fixing at the text stage is always the cheapest.
**Step 6: Review the cuts in Edit Panel (Panel and Sheet views)**
Generating images moves you to the **Edit Panel** stage. The **Panel / Sheet** buttons next to the model selector switch how you look at the result.

rows: One card per cut, with an Edit button, the scene description, dialogue and SFX under the image
Reading and fixing cuts one by one
All cut images in one large sheet, without the text
Seeing the whole flow at a glance

blocks.text: **Start with Sheet to read the flow.** Looking at the pictures alone, with no text, makes it easier to judge whether the cuts play like an actual video.

items: Is any cut out of order or missing?
Do neighbouring cuts connect naturally (costume, props, lighting, eyeline)?
Does the same person have the same face in every cut?

blocks.text: There are three buttons at the top right of the screen.

items: **Download CUT ZIP** (Panel view) / **Download Sheet** (Sheet view): download all cut images at once, or the sheet as one image. Useful for sharing a storyboard with teammates or a client.
**Regenerate images**: generate the images again. The button shows the credits it costs, so check before you press it.
**Clear Sheet**: empties the sheet. It may be hard to undo, so download first.

blocks.text: **Step 7: Fix only the cuts that need it**
Leave the good cuts alone and fix only the ones with problems. In **Panel view**, press **Edit** on the cut you want to change and you can revise that cut by itself. Each cut card has these tools.

rows: Add an element used by the cut
Download the cut image / replace it with an outside image

blocks.text: The upload button (up arrow) lets you drop a key image made in Turn straight into that cut. It is handy when a prompt will not produce the composition you want.
**Quick Edit**

items: Press **Edit** on the cut and check that the cut number at the top of the window (for example CUT 04) is the one you meant.
Add reference images under **Reference images** if you need them.
Write the change in one sentence in **Edit prompt**. You can point at a person with an @ token.
Check the target cut, the instruction and the credit notice, then press **Apply edit**.

blocks.text: **How to write the instruction**: state what changes and what stays. Example: "change only the glasses, keep the pose and the background". Example: "only @image1's expression becomes surprised, keep the pottery in hand and the background".
**Detailed Edit** is for changing the camera. Adjust three things on the right.

items: **Shot Size**: how much of the scene fills the frame (for example Extreme Wide Shot, Close-up)
**Camera Angle**: camera height and tilt (for example Low Angle, Dutch Angle)
**Camera Movement**: how the camera moves (for example Handheld, Track Out)

blocks.text: In the example screen, a tense close composition of "POV - Low Angle - Handheld" was rebuilt as "Extreme Wide Shot - Dutch Angle - Track Out": a wide, tilted frame with the camera pulling back. Check the settings and press **Regenerate**, and again watch the credits shown on screen.

**Reordering the reference images** The cast and background cards used to generate cuts are managed as lists. You can drag cast among cast and background among background to change the order, and **Reset to automatic selection** returns to the default selection. After reordering, regenerate the cut images for the change to take effect.
**Final check before you hand over to Seedance**
When the storyboard is finished you move to the video stage. Check the list below first.

items: Did you check in Sheet view that the cuts connect naturally?
Do the image and the description match on every cut?
Are the cast tokens correct on every cut?
Is any cut missing?
Do shot length, frame size, camera angle and camera movement match the intent of the cut?

blocks.text: The cut images you approve here become the reference for the video prompt. Fixing composition is cheapest at this stage: once you are in video, a composition fix means re-rolling the video several times.
**Common mistakes**

items: **Skipping the written storyboard and generating images straight away**: if the cut order is wrong, the images have to be made again.
**Registering the same person on several cards**: the tokens get confusing and faces get mixed.
**Writing only what changes in the edit instruction**: if you do not say what to keep, other parts change too.
**Regenerating cuts that already work**: pick the problem cuts and fix them with Edit in Panel view.
**Reviewing only in Panel view**: reading text makes it easy to miss whether the pictures actually connect. Always take the step of reading the pictures alone in Sheet view.
**Switching image models halfway**: the look can shift from cut to cut.

post/ai-video-9-cut-curse-fix.title: Nine Cuts Without the Curse: Five Steps That Keep AI Video Consistent
post/ai-video-9-cut-curse-fix.summary: Video AI does not remember the previous cut. Five steps: space in Turn, faces and framing in FLEXBOARD, then references and prompts to pin whatever has to stay consistent.

blocks.text: Hello, this is Jinseo Lee, CEO of Cubeberry, the team building XCONDA.

In the previous post, "The curse of nine cuts in AI video", we showed bandages switching to the wrong arm, blood stains disappearing and window frames changing from wood to metal as the video moved from cut to cut. We promised a follow-up with the fix.

**Here is the short answer.** Video AI does not remember the previous cut. So do not leave memory to the AI: decide it yourself and restate it on every cut. Space is fixed in Turn, faces and framing in FLEXBOARD, and anything that has to stay consistent is pinned with references and prompts. Everything below can be done with the tools XCONDA already has.
Why does the AI forget the previous cut?

Video AI draws every cut from scratch. It does not keep the fact that the tactical light on the rifle was switched on in the previous cut. Even if the prompt says "the same Hyunwoo", the AI simply imagines a picture that fits the name Hyunwoo. So the tactical light goes out, the radio moves to the other shoulder, and a jacket appears over a vest that never had one.

On a real drama set a person solves this. The set has a script supervisor. Cut by cut they note the actor's clothing, the rifle in hand, where the radio sits, which layers are worn, even how wet the costume is, and they match it before the next cut. Cuts do not jump because the actor has a good memory, but because somebody writes it down and compares.
AI video needs that role too. The five steps below are a way to split the script supervisor's job across XCONDA.
Step 1. Fix the space first: Turn

The window frame that changes on every cut usually comes from letting the AI re-imagine the space each time. Just as a real set is built first and shot inside for days, an AI video needs its space built first.

items: Put photos of the space into the Reference stage of Turn. You can add Front, Left, Right and Back photos, or use only a Description if you have no photos.
Press Generate to build a 360-degree virtual set, then set the camera position in 3D Preview.
Save the viewpoints the cuts need as Freeze Frames. Those images become the background reference for every cut.

blocks.text: <XCONDA "TURN" preview screen>
Here is how we use it on real work. This is the space of our Cold Site spin-off, built in Turn.

For the over-the-shoulder scene in Cold Site, build the room the heroine walks into in Turn first, then pull the view from the male lead's side and the view from the heroine's side out of the same set. It is one room with the camera moved, so the window frame has no reason to change.
Step 2. Write the state ledger first
This step is a habit, not a tool. And it has the biggest effect.

Before you build the scene, write down briefly what must not change during it. It is the script supervisor's sheet, written in advance. For scene 4 of our Division Zero (outside an abandoned warehouse, a rainy night) it looks like this.

rows: Fitted to every rifle and on from the first frame
Is the light visible in every cut?
Fixed to the character's right shoulder strap (screen left in a frontal shot)
Check the strap position on the key image
Hyunwoo leads, Junki and Agent 1 two metres behind on either side, Agent 2 3.5 metres behind
Check the four positions in the long shot
White shirt, black tie, black vest, black trousers, combat boots (no jacket)
Check colour and layers in every cut
Heavy rain, early winter so no breath vapour
Appears only in the last cut of scene 4, absent before that
Did it appear early in an earlier cut?

blocks.text: One thing to be careful about here. **Decide whether left and right mean "the character's" or "the screen's" and write that down.** A character's right shoulder strap appears on screen left in a frontal shot. Mix the two and people get confused, and the AI gets more confused. We write both: "the character's right shoulder strap (screen left in a frontal shot)".
This ledger is used as a checklist in steps 3 and 4, and copied into the prompt in step 5.
Step 3. Lay the key images out on one screen and compare: FLEXBOARD
Before you run video, pull every cut as an image first. When one cut is wrong the video has to be re-run whole, but an image only needs that one frame pulled again.

items: Put the scenario in and FLEXBOARD splits it into cuts and makes a key image for each. Up to 36 cuts fit on one screen.
Attach the cast photos as references and the same face runs from the first cut to the last. The Turn images from step 1 go in as background references too.
In the Sheet view, see all cuts at once and compare them with the state ledger from step 2.
Open only the wrong cuts in the Panel view and pull them again. Leave the rest alone.

blocks.text: Checking nine cuts as video takes ages just to find the wrong one. Laid out as images, it takes seconds. The point of this step is to keep the "15 to 20 minutes of fixing per cut" from the first post out of the video stage. You can also watch the Cold Site trailer being designed cut by cut in FLEXBOARD.

**If splitting a scenario into cuts is hard: the FLEXBOARD Claude skill**

Writing the prompt that goes into FLEXBOARD from scratch is not easy. We packaged the method we use in production as a Claude skill. Install the skill in Claude and paste in a scenario, and it builds two things at once.



The order follows a real production. First it locks the cast, background and prop references, then splits the cuts, and finally hands you a copy-ready file after your confirmation. It also checks that the cut lengths add up, that no single cut is crammed with too much action, and that the number of characters is right.

You can download the FLEXBOARD skill from "Download the FLEXBOARD skill" further down this article.
Step 4. Feed in references that carry the state: Seedance 2.5

Once the key images are final you move to video generation in XCONDA and use Seedance 2.5. What matters here is not feeding in "a photo of the character" but **"an image that has the state drawn into it"**. On Division Zero we do not just add Hyunwoo's face: we add the full-body board with the white shirt, black tie, black plate carrier vest and the rifle with its tactical light on.

items: Choose the reference mode (Ref-to-video). You can attach up to 30 images, 10 videos and 10 audio files at once.

References stay uploaded and can be switched on and off. Only the images ticked (check mark) in the Reference tab are numbered @Image1, @Image2 and enter generation. A cross means the image is kept but inactive for this run. Switch on only the references a cut needs and leave the rest waiting.

Cast, props and spaces you use often can be saved to the Asset Library and loaded straight into other scenes. On Division Zero we save the character boards for Hyunwoo and Minhee and load them scene by scene.

Add the key image you finalised in FLEXBOARD. On Division Zero, the cut that shows the diamond formation - Hyunwoo at the front, Junki and Agent 1 two metres behind on either side, Agent 2 covering 3.5 metres back - is the evidence of the state.

If a prop matters, add an image of the prop alone. The tactical light has to be on from the first frame, and the radio has to sit on the right shoulder strap. Details like these change less from cut to cut when you add a close-up of the rifle and of the strap as separate images.

In the prompt, type @ to say which reference is what. On Division Zero we split face and costume. For example: "@image1: Hyunwoo's face and hair only. @image2: Hyunwoo's costume only. The face follows @image1. @image4: only the seats and materials of the car interior, do not reference people or lighting" - every reference says what alone to reference. Split the roles like this and face, costume and background do not bleed into each other.

blocks.text: The FLEXBOARD launch advert was made this way. Fifteen key images went in as references, fifteen cuts of 30 seconds were generated in Seedance 2.5 in one run, then trimmed to 26 seconds.
Step 5. Move the ledger into the prompt and look once more before you assemble

Copy the ledger from step 2 into the prompt. A Seedance prompt takes up to 30,000 characters, so length is not a concern. Aspect ratio, resolution, duration and High Quality are chosen in the Options tab. The yellow High Quality button is on, and pressing it switches it off.
With the XCONDA prompt skill you can build a Seedance prompt from the key image and edit Korean and English side by side. Write the ledger in Korean and just confirm that the English carried it over.
When the video comes back, hold the ledger and look once more before you join the cuts.

items: Are the props in hand and around them unchanged?
Are the costume colour, buttons and sleeves the same?
Are the windows, doors and furniture in the background in the same place?
Is the number of people right in every cut?

blocks.text: If a cut is off, regenerate only that scene. Here too it costs fewer credits to go back to step 3, fix one key image and feed it in again than to rewrite the prompt and run it several times.

For scenes with complicated blocking - several characters crossing paths, for example - it helps to set the positions and paths first in the Blocking Board. The Blocking Board is now available on the web in XCONDA. We will cover how to use it in a separate post.
In summary

rows: Fix the space as a 360-degree set first
Window frames, walls and furniture changing
Record what has to stay the same in advance
Tactical lights, radios and costumes changing
Lay out key images, compare with the ledger, fix only the wrong cuts
Repeated regeneration at the video stage
Point at state-carrying images and prop images with @
Copy the ledger into the prompt and check before joining
Missed mismatches surviving into the final cut

blocks.text: The curse of nine cuts is not the AI being lazy. It comes from nobody remembering. Just as a drama set has a script supervisor, AI video needs an order for recording and comparing - and the cuts jump far less.
Download the FLEXBOARD skill
This is the FLEXBOARD Claude skill from step 3. Download the zip file below and install it in Claude. Do not unzip it: upload the zip as it is.

items: Download `flexboard-script-prompt.zip` below.
In Claude, open **Customize > Skills**.
Press **+**, choose **Create skill > Upload a skill**, and upload the zip file.
In a new chat, paste in a scenario and type "make me a written storyboard". If you call the skill without a scenario it first tells you what to prepare.

blocks.text: To close
I will finish with one finished piece made this way: the Cold Site spin-off trailer, every cut made with AI.

post/ai-video-background-consistency.title: Why AI video backgrounds jump — and how to hold cuts consistent
post/ai-video-background-consistency.summary: Why the background changes from cut to cut in AI video, and how to solve cut consistency, drawing on the ByteDance workshop and the Cubeberry pipeline.

blocks.text: Hello, this is XCONDA.
If you have made video with AI, you have met a fatal frustration at least once.

The first cut comes out exactly how you wanted, and then **from the second cut the background shifts subtly, the character's jawline changes, and the room you had is suddenly a completely different room**.
In the end you hit regenerate six, seven times to get the scene you want.
**More regenerations means a higher production cost.**
Every credit spent is money, so people do not experiment freely, and most end up never finishing even a single video.

On 31 July, Cubeberry CEO Jinseo Lee addressed exactly this 'cut consistency' problem at a **workshop of the Korea AI Drama Creators Association**. It was a diagnosis grounded in the field, from a PD with 28 years directing dramas at KBS.
"The line a director least wants to hear on set was 'the cut jumps'. And the very same problem turns up on AI video sets."
This post shares the key points and the fixes presented at that workshop.
Sponsoring the association workshop & Seedance 2.0 credits
On Friday 31 July 2026, the Korea AI Drama Creators Association workshop was held at the **ByteDance Korea office** in Gangnam, Seoul. Around 80 members attended.
Cubeberry took part as an official sponsor and provided attendees with **Seedance 2.0 credits** through the XCONDA platform, set up so people could try it hands-on on the spot.
CEO Jinseo Lee, who serves as a director of the association, explained why they supported the event.

"When I meet creators they say the same thing: AI tools are everywhere, but they have never carried one piece through to the end. I deeply related to the line that credits are too precious to press a single button.
A finished piece that pushes past the limits of AI video
👉 **Watch the <Cold Sight> spin-off trailer**
It adapts a disaster-SF original IP into the zombie genre. **Every cut was AI-generated**, with not a single live-action shot.

We are sharing Cubeberry's production pipeline: what was hard while making this trailer and how we solved it. The finished piece alone gets a "that looks good", but what matters is the part before it.
⚙️ Cubeberry's AI video production pipeline
Plaintext

[Space / cut consistency]
TURN (build the virtual set) ➔ FLEXBOARD (lock the key image per cut)

[Model use and generation]
Seedance 2.0 (feed the references) ➔ generate a 15-second clip ➔ repeat N times ➔ finish the feature trailer

items: **Seedance 2.0:** ByteDance's high-performance AI model
**TURN & FLEXBOARD:** Cubeberry's in-house causality-based directing engine
This was written against Seedance 2.0 at the time of the workshop; XCONDA now offers Seedance 2.5.

blocks.text: Fix ① Lock the space first — `TURN`
👉 **See how <Cold Sight> was built with TURN**

post/ontology-patent-cut-continuity.summary: AI video cannot remember the previous cut, so continuity breaks: shoes that were off are back on, a rain-soaked character is dry. We show a real cut that broke in an ad, the principle of the newly registered ontology patent, and the plan to apply it in FLEXBOARD.

blocks.text: Hello, this is XCONDA.

**Key summary** AI video cannot remember the previous cut, so when the cut changes, shoes that were kicked off are back on or a character soaked by rain is dry. Cubeberry registered an ontology-based patent for this problem (No. 10-3036790) on 19 October 2026. This post covers a real case from an ad, the principle of the patent, and the plan to apply it in FLEXBOARD.

**Before we start** The "continuity check" described here is a development plan. It is not in FLEXBOARD yet and no release date is fixed. The table below separates what you can use today from what is planned.
**Who this is for**: people bothered by props or costumes changing from cut to cut, people making drama or ads where cuts follow one another, and anyone curious about what Cubeberry has patented.
11 seconds and 23 seconds — the shoe came back
The ad above has a break in continuity. Look at two shots from the same ad side by side.

rows: A fish-eye shot holding both children together
Both feet in socks only; the shoes are on the ground
The last cut, lifting the flyer
One foot is wearing a shoe

blocks.text: Nothing in between shows the shoe being put back on. It is not a directing choice; it is a continuity error, created while generating 30 seconds in one pass. Because it was an ad, it shipped as it was.
This happens because video generation AI does not remember what happened in the previous cut — it draws every cut as if seeing the scene for the first time — so it can happen with any model.
In drama this is called "continuity"
Cubeberry CEO Jinseo Lee, who built XCONDA, directed dramas for 20 years as a PD. On set, continuity is one of the things you guard most carefully.

If an actor held a cup in the left hand and holds it in the right hand in the next cut, the screen jumps the moment the cut changes. The audience does not know why, but they sense "wait, something is off". Continuity missed on set surfaces in the edit room, and by then reshooting is hard. In drama it is an error that must not be allowed.
So we decided AI video also needs a device that says "continuity breaks here" first, and filed that method as a patent.
The patent registered this time

rows: A method for generating sequential content using ontology constraint-based violation verification and state transition propagation

blocks.text: Three principles in plain language

The name looks long and intimidating, but in set language it means "the system takes care of continuity". Below is a plain-language explanation of the concepts behind the title. It is not a legal reading of the claims.

**1. Build a rule book (ontology)**
Write down what characters, props, costumes and locations are, and which states each can be in — for example, "a shoe is either worn, taken off, or held in the hand".

**2. Catch rule violations before creating (violation verification)**
Cuts that do not add up — "a shoe kicked off is back on the foot in the next cut" — are filtered out before any video is made.

**3. Pass the changed state forward (state transition propagation)**
If a shoe comes off in cut 5, "socks only" carries from cut 6 to the last cut. A change that happened once, like a mark on a child's forehead from being hit by a shoe, follows into later cuts too.
The plan for FLEXBOARD

FLEXBOARD is convenient because you can pick one cut and regenerate it. But fixing cut 5 alone can leave cuts 6 to 10 no longer matching the fixed cut 5 — on set, the equivalent of one retake making every later scene's continuity jump. This patent is planned for FLEXBOARD in a direction that reduces that problem.

Frequently asked

**Q. Can I use the continuity check now?**
Not yet. It is at the planning stage and no release date is set. Anything marked "Available now" in the table above can be used right away.

**Q. How do I reduce cuts jumping today?**
Lock characters with Face Lock in FLEXBOARD, hold continuing states with references and prompts, and check that the pictures connect in Sheet view. The 5-step method is written up in the "curse of the 9 cuts" post below.

**Q. Is the error in the rice-paddy ad a Seedance problem?**
We do not see it as a problem of one model. Video generation AI works without remembering the previous cut, so it can happen with any model in a video where cuts follow one another.

blocks.text: Hello, this is XCONDA.

**Key summary** Generate ten AI videos and one or two are usable; the rest get thrown away and re-run. Cubeberry registered a patent (No. 10-3002930) for checking twice before rendering and telling the AI where, and by how much, something was wrong. This post covers the principle and the plan to bring it into XCONDA.
**Before we start** The verification and correction features described here are a development plan. They are not live in XCONDA yet and no release date is fixed.

**Who this is for**: people who resent burning credits picking one usable take out of many, people worn down by hands passing through tables or objects floating in mid-air, and anyone curious about what Cubeberry has patented.
Generate ten, keep one or two
Anyone who has made AI video knows. Generate ten and one or two are usable; the rest look like this.

items: A hand passes through a table.
A cup floats in mid-air.

blocks.text: So what do you do? Throw it away and run it again. Until it works.
This kept bothering CEO Jinseo Lee, because the cost of making the video is already spent by the time you throw it away. Work like that on a drama set and the producer yells at you.
On a drama set, checking comes first

Shooting a drama follows a fixed order. Check the storyboard, walk the blocking, and only then roll the camera. Checking first, shooting later. Over 20 years directing dramas as a PD, Jinseo Lee learned how much money that order saves.
This patent moves that order into AI.
Two checks before you render
Below is a plain-language explanation of the patent's concept. It is not a legal reading of the claims.

**First check: does it break the settings already decided?**
We see whether the scene fits the settings established in advance. An introverted character suddenly turning violent, or a car appearing in a medieval setting, is caught here.

**Second check: does the movement make physical sense?**
If it passes the first, we stand the people and objects up as simple shapes and turn them gently — a rehearsal before the shoot. Here we catch objects passing through each other, defying gravity, or movement that stops unnaturally. Because this happens before the real video, it costs almost nothing.

**When a problem is caught: tell, do not throw away**
When a problem is found, we do not just discard it. We extract where and how badly it went wrong and turn that into a form the AI can understand, then feed it back. The goal is for the same mistake not to happen in the same place next time.

post/scenario-to-final-video.title: From Scenario to Finished Video: XCONDA Production in 7 Steps
post/scenario-to-final-video.summary: Cubeberry's AI video starts from a scenario, is generated in XCONDA, gets sound from Suno and is finished in Premiere Pro. One map plus the seven steps: what goes in, what comes out, what to check.

blocks.text: **The AI video production workflow, EP.00: the whole map** - start here if this is your first read

Hello, this is XCONDA. Cubeberry's AI video starts from a scenario, is generated in XCONDA, gets sound from Suno, and is finished in Premiere Pro. This article shows the whole order as one map plus a step-by-step explanation. The details of each step follow in the series.

**In short** The whole thing is seven steps: preparation (01-04), video (05), finishing (06-07). For each step this article sets out what goes in, what comes out, and what to check before moving on. If you get stuck on a step, jump to the detailed post for it.
**Who it is for**: people making AI video for the first time, people who have used the tools but struggle to make cuts connect, and teams that need to share a production order.
The flow at a glance
**Scenario -> references -> written storyboard -> storyboard and blocking -> video generation -> sound -> edit and finish**

rows: Finalise the scenario that everything starts from
Make the reference images for cast and space (character sheets, background sheets)
Claude, Flexboard skill, GPT image, XCONDA Turn
Work out the cuts in text first
Check the key image for each cut and set the paths as video
Feed in everything from the previous steps and generate
Claude, Seedance prompt skill, prompt editor, XCONDA
Make the sound for the video
Put video and sound together to finish

blocks.text: On the map, the yellow outline marks 04 storyboard and blocking. It is the link between preparation and video: the output of the earlier steps gathers here, and the key images finalised here become the basis of the 05 prompt. If you dislike the result at 05, you fix the problem part and generate again - that loop is the normal way to work.
Why four steps of preparation before generating video?

Put text alone into video AI and you get a different face, different clothes and different framing every time. Join the cuts and it looks like a different actor in each one. The preparation steps pin that wobble down before any video is made.

The easiest comparison is how our CEO used to direct dramas at KBS. Before the camera rolls on set you cast the actors, build the set, and check cut order and framing on a storyboard. Fixing on paper costs almost nothing, while fixing after the shoot means shooting again. AI video also spends credits every time you run it. Checking a video with the wrong framing and starting over is the same as shooting the whole day again.
The key here is the division of labour between text and image. Each does what the other cannot.

rows: Cut order, framing, blocking, action, timing

blocks.text: However carefully you describe a face or an outfit in words, it never lands as precisely as an image, and cut order and timing are hard to convey with images. So cast and space are carried by images, and flow and movement by text.
Why cuts jump is covered in more depth at ‣, and the practical fix at ‣.
Step by step
Each step is set out as **input -> output -> check before moving on**. The check is what you verify yourself before going to the next step.
01. Write the scenario

items: **Input**: idea, pitch
**Output**: a final scenario
**Check**: are the characters and locations decided?

blocks.text: Everything starts here. If the characters and places are not settled you cannot make the references for the next step. Do not write an emotion as a label ("sad"); write a visible action such as "hides the shard of broken pottery behind her back", which makes splitting into cuts much easier later.
02. Get the reference images

items: **Tools**: Claude, the XCONDA Flexboard skill, GPT image, XCONDA Turn
**Input**: the scenario
**Output**: a face image per character (character sheet), location images (background sheets), and cut images made in Turn where needed
**Check**: does every character have a face image, is there a location image, and were the hard cuts made in Turn?

blocks.text: If you already have references, put them in with the scenario as they are. If not, the Flexboard skill reads the scenario and writes the prompts that create character sheets and background sheets. Copy those prompts, make the images in GPT image, then feed the images back in.

**Using XCONDA Turn: build two things from a 360-degree virtual set**
Turn builds a virtual set you can look around in 360 degrees from one photo or a text description. You build the space once and pick angles by moving the camera inside it, so doors, windows and props keep their positions across cuts.

**Method A. Make a background sheet**
1. Put one face of the background sheet (the front image) into Turn.
2. Build the left, right and back from that face.
3. Use the four faces together as the background reference. The result goes into 05 video generation as a background reference.

**Method B. Make storyboard cut images**
1. Build a 360-degree virtual set.
2. Place the cast and props inside the set.
3. Rotate to the angles you want and pull the cut images. The result goes straight into the 04 storyboard as cut images.

Why do it this way? Generate the background separately for each cut and the windows, furniture and props end up in different places in every cut. On a real set you build the set first and move only the camera inside it; the same idea: fix the space, then change the angle. Method B is especially useful when a composition is too complex for text alone and you want to place it yourself.
**Common mistake** Putting several face images of the same character in at once blends and smears the faces. One face image per character is the rule.
03. Written storyboard and Flexboard prompt

items: **Tools**: Claude, the XCONDA Flexboard skill
**Input**: the scenario and the reference images from 02
**Output**: a written storyboard (length, camera, action, dialogue, sound effects per cut) and a Flexboard prompt
**Check**: does every cut state a start action and an end action?

blocks.text: A written storyboard is the storyboard written out in text first. At this stage you also check that the cut lengths add up, that no cut crams in too much action, that cuts do not jump awkwardly, and that the number of characters is right. Where to download and install the skill is at the bottom of ‣.
04. Storyboard and blocking video

items: **Tools**: XCONDA FLEXBOARD, XCONDA Blocking Board
**Input**: the Flexboard prompt from 03, the cut images made in Turn at 02 (for the hard cuts)
**Output**: a key image per cut (storyboard images), a blocking puppet video
**Check**: is the key frame of each cut the framing you intended, and does the puppet video match the paths you meant?

blocks.text: FLEXBOARD is a storyboard tool that splits a scenario into cuts, makes an image for each, and lays them out on one screen. Up to 36 cuts fit on a screen, and you can leave the good cuts alone and fix only the ones with problems. The screen-by-screen walkthrough is at ‣.

**XCONDA Blocking Board: show the paths as video**
A movement like "enters from the left door, walks round the table and stands at the window" written only in text can send the model walking in the wrong direction. Scenes with several characters moving at once go wrong especially easily. The Blocking Board makes a video of grey mannequins (puppets) moving inside the space, and when you feed that video into generation, Seedance reads the paths as video rather than text.

That is the division of labour: faces and costume come from reference images, path and timing from the puppet video.

The Blocking Board is currently in free beta (up to the pre-generation stage). Paste a scene prompt and press Create to build the 3D space and the characters, add cameras with Add camera, then send to Seedance from the Output tab. See the notice at ‣ for the full introduction.
The puppet does not need to look human. Position, direction and speed are enough. Just remember to attach the puppet video when you generate at 05.
**Fixing here is the cheapest.** Generate video with the wrong framing and you will regenerate several times at the video stage. Fix it in the storyboard first.
05. Seedance prompt and video generation

items: **Tools**: Claude, the Seedance prompt skill, the prompt editor, XCONDA
**Input**: the Flexboard prompt and written storyboard, reference images, storyboard, the blocking puppet video from 04, and an audio reference if needed
**Output**: a two-column prompt editor with Korean and English side by side, and the video generated in XCONDA
**How to revise**: ask for the changes in conversation after seeing the result, let the editor revise, and generate again. Repeat until you are happy.

blocks.text: The Seedance prompt skill builds a Seedance 2.5 prompt from the key images. It organises it with a four-director system and a ten-block structure and lets you edit Korean and English side by side. Change the Korean and the English is rewritten to match, so you never edit English separately. This skill is being prepared for download from the XCONDA Hub.

**What goes into the XCONDA video generation screen: all four are required**

① **Reference images** (character sheets, background sheets, Turn sheets, props): they pin faces, costume and space.
② **Storyboard** (the cut images made at 04): it pins framing, paths and cut order.
③ **The Seedance prompt** (finished in the editor): it directs movement, timing and camera.
④ **The blocking puppet video** (made in the 04 Blocking Board): it pins the paths and routes of the characters.

If any one of the four is missing, the AI fills that part in as it likes. Leave out the reference images and even a prompt saying "@image1's woman" has no idea who that is, so faces differ from cut to cut. Leave out the storyboard and the framing changes every time even with the same prompt. Leave out the puppet video and characters walk in a different direction from the prompt, or several characters' paths cross each other.

In the generation screen you choose reference mode (Ref-to-video) and type @ in the prompt to say which reference is what. Aspect ratio, resolution, duration and High Quality are chosen in the Options tab, and Seedance 2.5 can make up to 30 seconds at a time.

In the stage where you revise and regenerate, the recently added Draft feature helps. Check the result as a 480p draft first and turn only the drafts you like into a 1080p final. The final is generated fresh from the same assets, so some fine detail may differ, and drafts stay valid for seven days after generation. See ‣ for details.
06. Sound

items: **Tool**: Suno
**Input**: the mood and length of the video finished at 05
**Output**: a sound file for the video
**Check**: does it match the length and mood of the video?

blocks.text: Sound is made after the video is finished, using the video's mood and length as the brief. The detail of this step follows in the series.
07. Combine video and sound

blocks.text: Hello, this is XCONDA.

**In short** Seedance 2.5 spends credits every time you run a video. So before you run video, build a cut-by-cut storyboard (key images) in FLEXBOARD and check it first. This article covers what FLEXBOARD is, what the screens look like, and how a scenario becomes a Seedance video in XCONDA, with real screens throughout.
**Who it is for**: anyone who has burned credits while running Seedance, anyone starting with AI video, and anyone whose faces change from cut to cut.
The advert at the top of this article was made this way: pull key images in FLEXBOARD, build the prompt with the XCONDA skill, then generate once in Seedance 2.5.
Why running video first feels expensive

Seedance 2.5 gives good results, and it costs credits every run. If the first video misses the intent, you have to run it again from the start: a character changed, the background jumped, the cut order feels off.
Checking as images costs far less than checking as video. Put the two side by side and the difference is clear.

rows: Watch the video to the end to find it
Lay the cuts out on one screen and see in seconds
Change the prompt and regenerate repeatedly
Grow a lot with every repeat

blocks.text: So before running video you need a stage where you look at "are these the right cuts?" as images. It is the same reason a drama set lines up the storyboard before the camera rolls.
FLEXBOARD is a storyboard engine

FLEXBOARD is a storyboard engine that turns a scenario into cut-by-cut images. Because it shows text and image together for every cut, you can check framing and characters before making video and fix only the cuts you do not like. It is designed to work with Seedance 2.5.
Open **Storyboard** in the left sidebar of XCONDA and the **Flex Board** card appears - the one labelled "a storyboard tool tuned for Seedance 2.5". Click it and choose **New Project**.
It was built around the places where video production usually stalls, and it has three core features.

items: **The same actor stays.** Face Lock keeps the same person across cuts. Cast and backgrounds are registered as cards, and each card automatically gets a label such as @image1 or @image2.
**Regenerate only the cut you want to change.** No rebuilding everything: just that cut.
**Choose the image model.** Pick from GPT Image 2, Seedream 5.0 Pro, GPT Image 2.5 Flare or GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst. If you are new, start with the default, GPT Image 2.

rows: 9 cuts x 15 seconds = about 2 minutes 15 seconds in simple total

blocks.text: FLEXBOARD on screen
Here are the key screens in the order you meet them. Step-by-step instructions are in FLEXBOARD storyboards in 7 steps.
**1) Enter the project and the scenario**

Set the working method, the model and the project name, then write the scenario. Do not name the emotion ("sad"); write a visible action such as "hides the shard behind her back", which is much easier to split into cuts.
**2) Register cast and background cards**
This is the step that keeps the same person and the same place across cuts. On a set it corresponds to casting and locking the set. Register one card per person.
**3) Set cut count and length, then read the written storyboard first**

Set the count in Number of Panels and the length in Shot Length. Then press **Text Preview Generate** and a written storyboard for each cut appears before any image is made. If the order or the cast feels wrong, fixing at this stage is fastest.
**4) Read the whole flow in Sheet view**

Generating images gives you a grid of cuts. **Sheet** view gathers the cut images large, without the text. Looking at the pictures alone makes it easy to judge whether the cuts flow like real video and whether costume and props changed.
**5) Fix only the cuts with problems**

This is the heart of FLEXBOARD. With Edit on a cut card you can make a quick fix of an expression or prop, or a detailed fix of the camera (Shot Size, Camera Angle, Camera Movement). Write both what changes and what stays: for example, "change only the glasses, keep the pose and the background".
Here is the same cut with a new composition: a tense POV frame rebuilt as a wide, tilted frame with the camera pulling back.
Two Claude skills work together
XCONDA has two skills for Claude.

**1. FLEXBOARD skill**
It cuts a scenario into shots. As it cuts, it checks that the shot lengths add up, that no shot crams in too much action, that cuts do not jump awkwardly, and that the number of characters is right. It returns a prompt to paste into FLEXBOARD together with a written storyboard listing length, camera, action, dialogue and sound effects for every cut.

**2. XCONDA prompt skill**
It builds a Seedance 2.5 prompt from the key images you pulled in FLEXBOARD. It organises the prompt with a four-director system and a ten-block structure, and lets you edit Korean and English side by side. Fix the Korean and the English is rewritten to match, so you never have to edit English separately.

blocks.text: Step 3 is the important one. If you finish the fixing at the image stage rather than the video stage, you run video fewer times. For scenes where several characters cross paths, it is steadier to set the paths first in the Blocking Board. For the whole picture from scenario to sound and editing, see one scenario to a finished video: the XCONDA production map in 7 steps, which lays it out as a single map.
How we made these
**The FLEXBOARD launch advert**

The advert at the top of this article put 15 key images in as references, generated 15 cuts of 30 seconds in Seedance 2.5 in one run, then trimmed it to 26 seconds. In the Seedance generation screen you choose reference mode (Ref-to-video) and type @ in the prompt to say which image is who and what.
**The Cold Site spin-off trailer**
The trailer with every cut made by AI was produced in the same order. You can watch the process of designing it cut by cut in FLEXBOARD.
The storyboard is what stops cuts from jumping

Video AI does not remember the previous cut. So when the cut changes, a bandage moves to the other arm, blood stains disappear and window frames change. Finding that after the video is finished is expensive; finding it at the storyboard stage costs one image.

Space in Turn, faces and framing in FLEXBOARD, and everything that must stay consistent pinned with references and prompts - that is written up as five steps in Nine cuts without the curse: how to cut it down with XCONDA today.
The same principle as an on-set storyboard

On drama sets it is common to shoot without a full read-through or a site visit, and to be handed last-minute pages. What sorts out the day's cuts quickly on location is the on-set storyboard. A storyboard cuts wasted trips, because fixing on paper before the camera rolls costs almost nothing, while fixing after the shoot means shooting again.
AI video is the same. Running video without a storyboard spends credits on wasted trips. FLEXBOARD is the on-set storyboard of AI video production.
Checklist before you hand over to Seedance

items: Did you check in Sheet view that the cuts connect naturally?
Do the image and the scene description match on every cut?
Are the cast tokens (@imageN) correct on every cut?
Is any cut missing?
Do shot length, frame size, camera angle and camera movement match the intent of the cut?

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Skipping the written storyboard and generating images.** If the cut order is wrong, the images have to be made again.
**Registering the same person on several cards.** Tokens get confusing and faces get mixed.
**Regenerating cuts that already work.** Pick only the problem cuts and fix them with Edit.
**Reviewing only in Panel view.** Reading text makes it easy to miss whether the pictures connect. Read the pictures alone in Sheet view.
**Switching image models halfway.** The look shifts from cut to cut, so stay with the model you chose.

blocks.text: Frequently asked questions

**Q. How many cuts, and how long, can FLEXBOARD make?**
Up to 36 cuts on one screen, and each cut can be set between 4 and 30 seconds.

**Q. How long a video can Seedance 2.5 make?**
Per the developer ByteDance Seed, up to 30 seconds of video with sound in one run. Aspect ratio, resolution and duration are chosen in the settings bar of the XCONDA video generation screen, and prompts can be up to 30,000 characters.

**Q. Where do I get the skills?**
The FLEXBOARD skill can be downloaded as a zip from the bottom of Nine cuts without the curse: how to cut it down with XCONDA today, and installed in Claude under Customize > Skills. post/xconda-production-map.title: From one scenario to a finished video: the XCONDA production map in 7 steps
post/xconda-production-map.summary: Cubeberry's AI video starts with a scenario, is produced in XCONDA, gets its sound in Suno and is finished in Premiere Pro. This post lays the whole order out as a single map, with the input, deliverable and checks for each step; the detailed how-tos continue in the series.

blocks.text: AI video production EP.00 — the full map. Start here if this is your first time.

Hello, this is XCONDA. Cubeberry's AI video starts with a scenario, is produced in XCONDA, gets its sound in Suno, and is finished in Premiere Pro. This post shows the whole sequence as one map, with an explanation for each step. The detailed method for every step continues in the series below.

Key summary: the process is 7 steps — preparation (01–04), video (05) and post (06–07). This post shows that order as a single map and sets out, for each step, what goes in, what comes out and what to check before moving on.
Who this is for: people making AI video for the first time, people who have used the tools but struggle to make cuts connect, and teams that need to share one production order.
How to read: if you are new, start here; when you get stuck on a step, jump to the detailed post for that step. The series keeps going, so this post doubles as a table of contents.
The flow at a glance
Scenario → references → text storyboard → storyboard and blocking → video generation → sound → edit and finish

rows: Lock the scenario that everything else starts from
Build the reference images for characters and spaces (character sheet, background sheet)
Claude, FLEXBOARD skill, GPT Image, XCONDA Turn
Write the cuts out in words first
Check the key image per cut and set the movement as video
Feed in every earlier output and generate the video
Claude, Seedance prompt skill, prompt editor, XCONDA
Make the sound for the video
Combine picture and sound to finish

blocks.text: The area outlined in yellow on the map is 04 storyboard and blocking, because it is the link between preparation and video work. The outputs of the earlier steps gather there, and the key images confirmed there become the basis for the prompts in 05. If you dislike the result at 05, you fix the problem area and generate again — that is where the flow turns into a loop.
Why four preparation steps before generating video?

Give a video AI nothing but text and you get a different face, different clothes and a different composition every time. Stitch the cuts together and it looks like a different actor performed each one. The preparation steps exist to lock that wobble down before any video is made.

The easiest analogy is our CEO's time directing dramas at KBS. On set you confirm the actors, build the set and check the order and framing of cuts on a storyboard before rolling the camera — because fixing things on paper costs almost nothing, while fixing them after the shoot means shooting again. AI video also spends credits every time you roll. Checking a badly framed video and starting over is the same as reshooting the entire scene.
The key here is the division of labour between text and images. Each does what the other cannot.

rows: Cut order, framing, movement, action, timing

blocks.text: However precisely you describe a face or an outfit in words, it never conveys what an image does, and conversely the order and timing of cuts are hard to convey with images. So characters and spaces are handled by images, and flow and movement by text.
Why cuts jump is covered in the post on background and cut consistency, and practical fixes in the guide to the 9-cut curse.
Step by step
Each step is laid out as input → deliverable → check before moving on. The check is what you verify yourself before going on to the next step.
01. Write the scenario

items: Input: idea, proposal
Deliverable: a locked scenario
Check before moving on: are the characters and locations decided?

blocks.text: Everything starts here. Without characters and locations you cannot build the references for the next step. Rather than naming an emotion ("sad"), write it as something visible — "hides the broken shard behind her back" — so it is easier to break into cuts later.
02. Get the reference images

items: Tools: Claude, the XCONDA FLEXBOARD skill, GPT Image, XCONDA Turn
Input: the scenario
Deliverable: a face image per character (character sheet), location images (background sheets), and cut images made in Turn where needed
Check before moving on: does every character have a face image, do you have the location images, and did you build the hard-to-shoot cuts in Turn?

blocks.text: If you already have references, use them as they are alongside the scenario. If not, the FLEXBOARD skill reads the scenario and writes the prompts that make a character sheet and a background sheet. Copy those prompts into GPT Image to make the images, then feed the images back in.

Using XCONDA Turn: two things from a 360° virtual set. Turn builds a virtual set you can look around 360° from a single photo or a text description. Because you build one space first and then turn the camera inside it to pick angles, doors, windows and props stay in place as the cuts change. Method A — build a background sheet: 1) put one face of the background sheet (the front image) into Turn. 2) Build the left, right and back sides from it. 3) Use the four sides together as the background reference; this feeds the background reference for 05 video generation. Method B — build storyboard cut images: 1) create the 360° virtual set. 2) Place characters and props inside it. 3) Turn to the angle you want and pull the cut image; this goes straight into the 04 storyboard as a cut image.

Why do it this way? Generate the background separately for each cut and the windows, furniture and props move from cut to cut. On a real set you build the set once and only move the camera inside it — the same idea: fix the space first, then change the angle. Method B is especially useful when you want to place a complex composition yourself, because text alone rarely produces it.
Common mistake: putting several face images of the same person in at once blends and smears the face. The rule is one face image per character.
03. Text storyboard and FLEXBOARD prompts

items: Tools: Claude, the XCONDA FLEXBOARD skill
Input: the scenario and the reference images from 02
Deliverable: a text storyboard (length, camera, action, dialogue and sound effects per cut) and the prompts for FLEXBOARD
Check before moving on: does every cut state a start action and an end action?

blocks.text: A text storyboard is the scene written out in words first. At this stage you also check that the cut lengths add up, that no single cut is crammed with action, that cuts do not jump awkwardly, and that the number of characters is right. Where to download and install the skills is covered lower down.
04. Storyboard and blocking video

items: Tools: XCONDA FLEXBOARD, XCONDA Blocking Board
Input: the FLEXBOARD prompts from 03, and the cut images made in Turn at 02 (the hard-to-shoot cuts)
Deliverable: a key image per cut (storyboard images) and a blocking puppet video
Check before moving on: is each cut's key frame the composition you intended, and does the puppet video's movement match your intent?

blocks.text: FLEXBOARD is a storyboard tool that splits the scenario into cuts, generates an image for each cut and lays them out on one screen. It holds up to 36 cuts on a screen, and you can leave the good cuts alone and fix only the ones with problems. The click-by-click walkthrough is written up in the FLEXBOARD guide.

XCONDA Blocking Board: showing character movement as video. Movement like "enters through the left door, walks around the table and stops at the window" invites the model to walk the wrong way when it is only written down, and scenes with several characters moving at once drift easily. Blocking Board produces a video of grey mannequins (puppets) moving inside the space; add that video to video generation and Seedance reads the movement from video rather than text. The division of labour: reference images handle faces and costumes, the puppet video handles paths and timing.

Blocking Board is currently open as a free beta (up to the stage before video generation). Paste a scene prompt and press Create to compose the 3D space and characters, add cameras with Add camera, and send to Seedance from the Output tab. See the Blocking Board beta notice for the full introduction.
The puppet does not need to look human. Position, direction and speed are enough. Just remember to attach the puppet video at 05 video generation.
Fixing here is the cheapest. Generate video with the wrong composition and you regenerate several times at the video stage. Fix it in the storyboard first.
05. Seedance prompts and video generation

items: Tools: Claude, the Seedance prompt skill, the prompt editor, XCONDA
Input: the FLEXBOARD prompts and text storyboard, reference images, the storyboard, the blocking puppet video from 04, and audio references if needed
Deliverable: a two-column prompt editor with Korean and English side by side, and the video generated in XCONDA
How to revise: tell the editor in conversation what to fix, it updates the prompt, and you generate again. Repeat the loop until you are happy.

blocks.text: The Seedance prompt skill builds prompts for Seedance 2.5 from the key images. It organises them with a four-director system and a ten-block structure, and lets you revise with Korean and English side by side. Revise in Korean and the English is rewritten to match, so you never have to edit the English separately. The skill is being prepared for download from the XCONDA hub.

What goes into the XCONDA video generation screen: all four are required. ① Reference images (character sheets, background sheets, Turn sheets, props): they fix faces, costumes and spaces. ② The storyboard (the per-cut images made at 04): it fixes composition, movement and cut order. ③ The Seedance prompt (finished in the editor): it directs movement, timing and camera. ④ The blocking puppet video (made in Blocking Board at 04): it fixes the character's path and travel route.

If any one of the four is missing, the AI fills that part in as it likes. Drop the reference images, for example, and even if the prompt says "the woman in @image1" it cannot tell who that is, so the face changes from cut to cut. Drop the storyboard and the composition changes every time even with the same prompt; drop the puppet video and characters walk in a different direction from the prompt, or several characters' paths cross each other.

On the generation screen, choose Reference (Ref-to-video) mode and type @ in the prompt to say which reference is which. Aspect ratio, resolution, length and High Quality are set on the Options tab, and Seedance 2.5 can produce up to 30 seconds at a time.

While you iterate on revisions and regenerations, the recently added Draft feature helps: check the result at 480p first and turn only the drafts you like into 1080p finals. Note that the final is generated fresh from the same assets as the draft, so fine details can differ slightly, and drafts are valid for 7 days after generation. See the Draft notice for details.
06. Sound

items: Tools: Suno
Input: the mood and length of the video finished at 05
Deliverable: sound files for the video
Check before moving on: does it match the video's length and mood?

blocks.text: Sound is made after the video is finished, using the video's mood and length as the brief. The detailed method for this step continues in the series.
07. Combine video and sound

items: Tools: Premiere Pro
Input: the clips generated at 05 and the sound made at 06
Deliverable: the finished video
Check before moving on: cut connections, levels and subtitles

blocks.text: The last step. Before joining the cuts, keep the references from 02 and the text storyboard from 03 beside you and run through once more to confirm that costumes, props and backgrounds do not change from cut to cut.

So you can check as you read the map, the input, deliverable and pre-handover checks are gathered in one table.

Does every character have a face image, do you have the location images, and did you build the hard cuts in Turn?

blocks.text: Five common mistakes

items: Generating video first: check with images and you only redo the one wrong cut. With video you redo the whole thing.
Adding several face images of the same character: the faces blend. One per character is the rule.
Putting only some of the four inputs into generation: whatever is missing — references, storyboard, prompt or puppet video — the AI fills in as it likes.
Expecting faces and expressions from the puppet video: puppets carry position, direction and speed only. Faces belong to the reference images.

qna/flexboard-character-consistency.title: How do I keep the same character across shots?
qna/flexboard-character-consistency.summary: Register a character (Cast) card and a background card under Reference Assets in Scene Settings. Each card carries a token such as @image1 or @image2, and including that token in a shot description shows which character and background were used. Register one card per character.

qna/flexboard-cut-count-and-length.title: How many shots can FLEXBOARD hold, and how long can each be?

qna/flexboard-download-storyboard.title: Can I download the storyboard I made in FLEXBOARD?

qna/flexboard-edit-single-cut.title: Can I fix just one shot I don't like?
qna/flexboard-edit-single-cut.summary: Yes. In Edit Panel's Panel view, press Edit on the shot you want to change and only that shot is revised. For a simple change, write one sentence in Quick Edit (for example, "change only the glasses, keep the pose and background"). To change the camera, pick Shot Size, Camera Angle and Camera Movement in Detailed Edit and regenerate. Every other shot stays as it is.

qna/flexboard-panel-vs-sheet.title: What is the difference between Panel and Sheet view?
qna/flexboard-panel-vs-sheet.summary: Panel view shows one card per shot with its image, scene description, dialogue, sound cues and an Edit button — use it to read and fix individual shots. Sheet view shows the shot images large, without descriptions — use it to judge whether the sequence flows. The recommended order is Sheet first for flow, then Panel shot by shot.

qna/mixing-with-live-footage.title: Can I mix live-action footage with AI video?

qna/seedance-2-5-length-resolution.title: What length and resolution can Seedance 2.5 produce?
qna/seedance-2-5-length-resolution.summary: In the XCONDA Video Generator, choosing Seedance 2.5 lets you generate from text, images, start and end frames, or references (Ref-to-video). Per the model's developer ByteDance Seed, Seedance 2.5 produces up to 30 seconds of video with audio in one pass. Results record resolution, aspect ratio and length — for example 720P, 16:9, 20 or 27 seconds — so you can set the duration to the second. The settings bar under the prompt box controls aspect ratio (e.g. 16:9), resolution (e.g. 720p), length (e.g. 20s) and High Quality, and prompts can be up to 30,000 characters. Available values are listed in each settings menu.

qna/seedance-prompt-language.title: Do I have to write prompts in English?
qna/seedance-prompt-language.summary: With the XCONDA Prompt skill you edit prompts in a side-by-side Korean and English editor. Check the meaning in Korean, then paste the English working version into video generation. You do not need to write English yourself.

qna/seedance-prompt-retry.title: Do I have to rewrite the prompt from scratch if I dislike the result?
qna/seedance-prompt-retry.summary: No. In the XCONDA Prompt skill you tell it in conversation what to fix, the prompt in the editor is updated, and you generate again with it. Repeat until the shot reaches the standard you want.

qna/seedance-reference-limits.title: How many reference images and videos can I add?
qna/seedance-reference-limits.summary: In the Reference mode of XCONDA video generation you can add up to 30 images, 10 videos and 10 audio clips at a time. Assets you add are kept in the Input Assets library, and you type @ in the prompt to point at the asset you mean.

qna/skills-claude-paid-plan.title: Do I need a paid Claude plan to use the skills?
qna/skills-claude-paid-plan.summary: Anthropic's help centre states that skills are available on the Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans, with code execution enabled in settings. Usage limits differ by plan, so a paid plan is easier if you work on long scenarios often. Claude's policy can change — check the Claude help centre for the current rules.

qna/sound-and-editing.summary: In Cubeberry's production flow, sound is created in Suno to match the mood and length of the finished video, then video and sound are combined in Premiere Pro, where cuts, levels and subtitles are checked before final output.

qna/subscription-auto-renewal.title: Does a subscription renew automatically?
qna/subscription-auto-renewal.summary: Yes. Until you cancel, a subscription is charged automatically each month on the same date to the stored payment method. Before the first payment we show the price, billing cycle, renewal terms and how to cancel, and you agree to them; after purchase we send a confirmation email with the renewal terms and cancellation steps.

qna/subscription-credit-rollover.title: Do unused subscription credits roll over to the next month?
qna/subscription-credit-rollover.summary: Yes. Unused subscription credits roll over to the next billing cycle and are valid for up to one year from the date they were granted. Expired credits lapse automatically, and credits are consumed starting with the earliest expiry date.

qna/supported-ai-models.title: Which AI models can I use?
qna/supported-ai-models.summary: Video generation supports Seedance 2.5, and Cubeberry is an Authorized Dealer for BytePlus. Image models differ by tool: in FLEXBOARD you can choose among GPT Image 2, Seedream 5.0 Pro, GPT Image 2.5 Flare and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, and in Turn between Gemini 3.1 Flash and GPT Image 2. Supported models change with releases — check each tool's screen for the current list.

qna/terms-change-notice.title: Will you tell me in advance if prices or terms change?
qna/terms-change-notice.summary: Yes. Price changes are announced 30 days before they take effect, and amounts already paid are charged at the old price. For subscriptions, the new price applies from the first billing date after the notice period, and you can cancel before then. Changes to the terms are announced 7 days in advance (30 days for changes unfavourable to members), and material changes to the privacy policy at least 30 days in advance.

qna/turn-image-usage.title: Where do images made in Turn get used?
qna/turn-image-usage.summary: Three places. Empty-space images (Freeze Frame) become background references for Seedance video generation; key images with a character become FLEXBOARD storyboard shots; and the space image becomes the stage for blocking in Blocking Board.

qna/turn-props-wallpaper.title: Can I add props or change wallpaper in Turn?
qna/turn-props-wallpaper.summary: Yes. In Wall Edit, choose one of the six direction cards, upload a reference image, paint the area you want to change and run it. Use INPAINT for a single prop (only the painted area is edited), REGEN to regenerate a whole wall of that direction, and REPLACE to swap a specific object. For broad surfaces such as wallpaper, pair the reference image with an instruction like "remove the moulding and change only the wallpaper" for a clean result.

qna/turn-room-size-credits.title: Does changing the room size in Turn cost more credits?
qna/turn-room-size-credits.summary: No. Change the room's width, depth and ceiling height in Room Size · Camera, then press "Apply Room Size · No Additional Generation" — the proportions change using the existing wall images without generating new ones, and props stay in place.

qna/turn-without-photos.title: Can I use Turn without any photos?
qna/turn-without-photos.summary: Yes. Leave all four reference slots (Front, Left, Right, Back) empty and the space is built from your written description alone. One front photo is also enough, and you can add photos of whichever directions you have.

qna/uploaded-content-usage.title: Does Cubeberry use the images and videos I upload?
qna/uploaded-content-usage.summary: You own the images and videos you upload and the work you create. Cubeberry may use that content to provide and improve the service. It is used to train XCONDA models only with your consent. We do not sell personal data and do not share it for targeted advertising.

qna/video-generation-inputs.title: What should I put into the video generation screen?
qna/video-generation-inputs.summary: Four things together: 1) reference images (character sheet, background sheet, props) to pin faces, wardrobe and space; 2) a storyboard (per-shot images) to pin framing and shot order; 3) a Seedance prompt in English for movement, timing and camera; 4) a blocking puppet clip to pin blocking and movement paths. Whatever you leave out, the model fills in on its own.

qna/what-is-blocking-board.title: What is Blocking Board?
qna/what-is-blocking-board.summary: Blocking Board is a digital rehearsal tool that checks whether people, space and camera work together before you generate video; it will be offered on the web. You draw character positions and movement paths on a floor plan, play the scene on a 3D stage and check sight lines, the 180-degree line and collisions. It can also export a clip of puppets moving through the space, which you can feed into video generation.

qna/what-is-flexboard.title: What is FLEXBOARD?
qna/what-is-flexboard.summary: FLEXBOARD is a storyboard tool that splits a scenario into shots and previews each shot with text and an image. You check framing and characters before generating video, then fix only the shots you dislike. It is designed to be used together with Seedance 2.5.

qna/what-is-turn.title: What is Turn?
qna/what-is-turn.summary: Turn builds a virtual set you can orbit 360 degrees from a single photo or a written description. Because you create one space and rotate the camera inside it, doors, windows and props stay where they were as shots change. You can add a character at the angle you like and produce key images from it.

qna/what-is-xconda.title: What is XCONDA?
qna/what-is-xconda.summary: XCONDA is an AI video and image production platform run by Cubeberry (xconda.ai). It gives you several generative models in one place plus production tools — FLEXBOARD, Turn, Blocking Board and others — that carry a project from scenario to storyboard to generated video. The focus is not a single clip but work in which many shots hold the same characters in the same space.

qna/what-is-xconda-claude-skill.title: What is an XCONDA skill for Claude?
qna/what-is-xconda-claude-skill.summary: A skill is a task tool for XCONDA work that you add to Claude. There are two. The FLEXBOARD skill splits a scenario into shots and checks the total running time, how much action each shot carries, whether similar shots sit next to each other and jar, and how many characters are on screen. The XCONDA Prompt skill builds Seedance 2.5 prompts from the key images you locked in FLEXBOARD, written as if four directors — overall, camera, lighting and art — each had a say.

qna/where-to-get-skills.title: Where do I get the skills?
qna/where-to-get-skills.summary: The Claude skills for the XCONDA production workflow (FLEXBOARD skill and XCONDA Prompt skill) are downloaded from the XCONDA hub. Add the downloaded file to Claude using the installation steps.

qna/who-made-xconda.title: Who made XCONDA?
qna/who-made-xconda.summary: XCONDA is developed and operated by Cubeberry Co., Ltd., based in Korea. Cubeberry was founded in 2023 and designed by CEO Jinseo Lee, a former KBS drama PD, together with a broadcast writer, working directors and AI video artists. The XCONDA pipeline produced KBS 1TV's "Legend of the Haunted: Gumiho" (May 2025 — the first AI animation broadcast in prime time by a Korean broadcaster), KBS documentary "Korean War Mobile Trauma Centre" (June 2025) and the generative AI parts of KBS 1TV documentary "Sacred Object" (aired March 2026), and is producing four AI web dramas in KOCCA's New Media Technology Content Lab. qna/why-faces-change-between-cuts.title: Why does the face change from shot to shot in AI video?
qna/why-faces-change-between-cuts.summary: Given only text, a video model imagines each frame anew, so faces, clothing and framing drift even when you describe the same character. Anything that must stay the same has to be pinned visually: faces and wardrobe with reference images, the space with a background image, and framing with a storyboard. XCONDA's workflow is built so that pinning happens before video generation.

qna/why-puppet-video.title: Why do I need a puppet clip?
qna/why-puppet-video.summary: Movement like "enters through the left door, walks around the table and stops by the window" often goes the wrong way when written as text, and several characters moving at once is hard to control in words. Adding a puppet clip lets Seedance read the blocking from video rather than text. The puppet does not need to look human — position, direction and speed are enough.

qna/xconda-video-workflow-overview.title: What is the full workflow for making a video with XCONDA?
qna/xconda-video-workflow-overview.summary: Cubeberry's production flow has seven steps: 1) write the scenario; 2) secure reference images (character sheet, Turn backgrounds); 3) write the written board and storyboard prompts (FLEXBOARD skill); 4) build the storyboard and blocking clip (FLEXBOARD, Blocking Board); 5) write the Seedance prompts and generate video; 6) produce sound; 7) combine video and sound. Step 4, the storyboard, is where preparation hands over to generation. The hub blog post "From one scenario to a finished video" walks through it.

qna/xconda-vs-other-ai-video-tools.title: How is XCONDA different from other AI video tools?
qna/xconda-vs-other-ai-video-tools.summary: XCONDA puts more weight on the stage before generation. Give a video model text alone and faces, wardrobe and framing drift from shot to shot. XCONDA's workflow pins faces, space, framing and blocking first — with FLEXBOARD (per-shot storyboard), Turn (360° virtual set) and Blocking Board (movement paths) — and then generates video. It is broadcast drama practice transferred to AI video.
